idiom_name: Spring Cloud Stream Rabbit binder autoBindDlq/republishToDlq (<destination>.dlq), or Spring AMQP QueueBuilder.deadLetterExchange
implementation_notes: Kotlin server code runs on the JVM, so the dead-letter channel comes from Spring. With the Spring Cloud Stream Rabbit binder, autoBindDlq=true makes the binder declare the dead-letter exchange and a queue named <destination>.dlq, and failed messages land there after the retry budget (maxAttempts) is exhausted - or immediately when retry is disabled and requeueRejected=false, which is the default; republishToDlq decides whether the binder republishes the failed message (preserving headers, and joining the transaction when the consumer is marked transacted) or rejects it and lets the broker dead-letter it. The framework explicitly provides no standard way to consume dead letters, so the triage listener on <destination>.dlq is application code. With plain Spring AMQP the same structure is spelled QueueBuilder.deadLetterExchange(...) plus a @RabbitListener on the DLQ; on the pure-coroutine side a kotlinx.coroutines Channel has no dead-letter concept at all, so a failure sink must be built by hand or work is lost silently.
pitfalls: With maxAttempts=1 and requeueRejected left true, a rejected message is requeued forever and never reaches the DLQ; requeueRejected=false is what makes the binder route it.
The binder creates the DLQ but no consumer for it - the reference documentation says so explicitly - so a <destination>.dlq with no listener is the normal failure mode.
Publishing to the DLQ from a transacted consumer only participates in the transaction when the binding is transacted; otherwise the original can be acked while the DLQ publish fails.
kotlinx.coroutines Channels drop or suspend instead of dead-lettering: an in-process pipeline needs its own bounded buffer plus an explicit failure sink, or failed elements simply disappear.
